meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We Can Complain Because Rose Bushes Have Thorns, or Rejoice Because Thorn Bushes Have Roses'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lincoln. The oldest version is a French quatrain Alphonse Karr printed in 1853 — and printed as anonymous. Lincoln's name was attached in 2003.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — an anonymous saying, traced back to Alphonse Karr
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence that Lincoln ever wrote or spoke this line, and traced the oldest version of the thought to a four-line French verse Alphonse Karr printed in his 1853 book Lettres écrites de mon jardin — a verse Karr introduced as though its author preferred to stay anonymous. The familiar English wording is later and anonymous still: its closest early appearance is a 1936 newspaper column that credited only “a philosopher.” Lincoln’s name was not attached to it until 2003.
answer.confidenceText: No known originator. Karr is the earliest documented source and the point at which the idea spread; the English sentence itself has never been traced to anyone.

source.heading: The oldest version anyone has found

docMeta.dd: Michel Lévy Frères, Paris, 1853 — the verse is on page 293
No period English translation of the verse. The familiar English sentence is a separate, later paraphrase with no known author.
Nobody. Karr presents the four lines as an author’s who would rather stay anonymous.

source.excerpt:
De leur meilleur côté tâchons de voir les choses :
Vous vous plaignez de voir les rosiers épineux ;
Moi je me réjouis et rends grâces aux dieux
Que les épines aient des roses.

Let us try to see things from their better side:
You complain about seeing thorny rose bushes;
Me, I rejoice and give thanks to the gods
That thorns have roses.
trail: 1853 — the oldest known version, and it is in French. Alphonse Karr ends a passage about gardeners’ roses with a four-line verse on page 293 of Lettres écrites de mon jardin ↗: others complain that rose bushes are thorny, he gives thanks that thorns have roses. He reprinted it in Sur la plage in 1862, and a collection of his sayings carried it without introduction in 1877.

1882 — it enters English, credited to Karr. Quote Investigator records the London Unitarian journal The Christian Life printing it as a remark of Alphonse Karr’s about finding fault with Nature for putting thorns on roses ↗. Other journals repeated it through the 1880s; by 1897 one had reassigned it to an unnamed German writer.

1936 — the modern wording appears, credited to nobody. The syndicated column “Office Cat” by Junius printed a version that QI calls similar to the saying people quote today ↗, attributing it only to “a philosopher.” The rose-bush-versus-thorn-bush pairing had surfaced in Roe Fulkerson’s newspaper column in 1929.

2003 — Lincoln’s name is attached. QI identifies the collection Wilderness Wisdom: Quotes for Inspirational Exploration, edited by John Gookin, as the point at which a version of the saying was assigned to Abraham Lincoln ↗. Nothing earlier connects him to it.
source.excerptNote: The English rendering is the one Quote Investigator gives ↗, prepared with help from two correspondents it credits by name; it is a plain translation of the French, not a historical English version. In the scanned original, Karr introduces the quatrain by saying he is slipping in four lines about roses and their thorns whose author wishes to seem to want anonymity — which is why QI treats the verse as having no acknowledged owner even at its first appearance. Note that Karr’s image is a single plant: a rose bush that has thorns. The two-bush version everybody quotes today came later, and in English.

source.rightsNote: The exact English sentence has no identifiable author, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it — its closest early appearance is an anonymous 1936 newspaper column crediting “a philosopher.” The French quatrain shown above is a different matter: first published in 1853, it is comfortably in the public domain, as is the 1882 English paraphrase credited to Karr. The modern English translation of the verse reproduced here is the one Quote Investigator published in 2013 and is quoted as fair comment on their research, not as a public-domain text.

author.name: Alphonse Karr
author.kicker: The gardener-journalist behind the oldest known version
author.heading: Who Alphonse Karr actually was
author.metaLine: 1808–1890 · French critic, journalist and novelist; editor of Le Figaro
author.bio: Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr was a French critic, journalist and novelist who became editor of Le Figaro in 1839 and founded the satirical monthly Les Guêpes. In 1855 he moved to Nice, took up floriculture, and practically founded the cut-flower trade on the French Riviera — which is why so many of his best-remembered lines are about gardens. He is the same writer who gave us plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose, and, characteristically, he printed the roses-and-thorns verse as if it were somebody else’s.

copyAttribution: Not Abraham Lincoln. The oldest known version is a French quatrain in Alphonse Karr, "Lettres écrites de mon jardin" (Paris: Michel Lévy Frères, 1853), p. 293 — which Karr printed as anonymous. The familiar English wording has no known author; Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence Lincoln ever wrote or spoke it, and dates the Lincoln attribution to 2003. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them right
misattribution.intro: This saying has been handed to at least three different people, and the evidence for each gets thinner the more famous the name.

items.why: Quote Investigator states it has located no substantive evidence that Lincoln wrote or spoke this quotation ↗, and dates the attribution to a 2003 collection, Wilderness Wisdom: Quotes for Inspirational Exploration, edited by John Gookin. Lincoln did once pair roses with thorns — in his 1850 eulogy for Zachary Taylor, saying the Presidency is no bed of roses and that General Taylor, like others, found thorns within it ↗. That is a complaint about political office, not a maxim about optimism.

A filler item in a Canton, Ohio newspaper credited “Morley” in April 1949, and the columnist Earl Wilson printed the fuller name in 1964 — both documented by Quote Investigator ↗. But the saying was already in print in 1936 credited to an unnamed “philosopher,” so the Morley credit post-dates the wording it is supposed to explain.

Karr is where the trail genuinely starts, and Victorian journals from 1882 onward credited him by name. But in the 1853 book itself ↗ he slips the four lines in with a remark that their author would rather appear anonymous — so even the earliest source declines to claim it.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that the saying has no known originator, though Karr was the primal locus of popularization ↗, and that the Lincoln attribution is recent and unsupported.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Lincoln
lead: The saying has an unusually well-documented life for something nobody can claim. It begins as a French joke about gardening, becomes a Victorian aphorism about Nature, passes through Unitarian journals, an evangelist’s prize contest and a lecture on the happiness habit, then a newspaper humour column, gets pinned on a man nobody can identify, and only then — in 2003, in a book of inspirational quotations for backpackers — arrives at Abraham Lincoln.

That last step is the giveaway. Lincoln is one of the internet’s great quotation magnets: a line that sounds wise, sounds American, and has no owner tends to drift toward him. What makes this case unusual is that the drift is fully visible. Quote Investigator can show you every stop on the route, and Lincoln appears at none of them until a century and a half of circulation had already happened without him.
context.detailsSummary: The wording changed at every stop
detailsBody: Karr’s 1853 quatrain is about thorns having roses — the plant is a rose bush either way, and the trick is which feature you notice. The 1882 English version in the London journal The Christian Life keeps that structure: finding fault with Nature for putting thorns on roses, versus thanking her for putting roses on thorns.

The two-bush version — a rose bush set against a thorn bush, as if they were different plants — is a twentieth-century American invention. Quote Investigator points to Roe Fulkerson’s 1929 newspaper column as the place those two terms first appear together, and to a 1936 “Office Cat” column for the first instance close to the sentence people quote today.

By 1949 a filler item in a Canton, Ohio paper was crediting it to “Morley,” and by 1964 the columnist Earl Wilson had expanded that to “J. Kenfield Morley” — a name that appears in quotation books and almost nowhere else. Lincoln arrives last.
context.pull: Karr wrote the oldest version and then pretended he hadn’t. Everyone since has been happy to hand it to someone else too.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Abraham Lincoln. No originator is known: the oldest documented version is a French quatrain Alphonse Karr printed in 1853, which Karr introduced as an author’s who wished to remain anonymous. Quote Investigator calls Karr the primal locus of popularization, not the author, and the familiar English wording has never been traced to anyone.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator located no substantive evidence that Abraham Lincoln wrote or spoke this quotation; the saying has no known originator; Karr was the primal locus of popularization; the Lincoln attribution occurred very recently and is unsupported, first appearing in the 2003 collection Wilderness Wisdom edited by John Gookin. QI also documents the 1853 Karr verse, the 1862 Sur la plage reprint, the 1877 L'esprit d'Alphonse Karr printing, the 1882 Christian Life English version, the 1929 Roe Fulkerson column, the 1936 Office Cat column by Junius crediting 'a philosopher', the 1949 Canton credit to 'Morley', and the 1964 Earl Wilson credit to J. Kenfield Morley.

Page 293 of the 1853 first edition of Alphonse Karr's Lettres écrites de mon jardin (Michel Lévy Frères, Paris) contains the quatrain 'De leur meilleur côté tâchons de voir les choses / Vous vous plaignez de voir les rosiers épineux ; / Moi je me réjouis et rends grâces aux dieux / Que les épines aient des roses.'

The Internet Archive holds a full scan of the 1853 Lettres écrites de mon jardin whose OCR text contains the quatrain on page 293, preceded by Karr's introductory line stating he is slipping in four lines about roses and their thorns whose author wishes to appear to want to remain anonymous.

Wikiquote's Alphonse Karr page carries the English rendering of the verse ('Let us try to see things from their better side: You complain about seeing thorny rose bushes; Me, I rejoice and give thanks to the gods That thorns have roses.') sourced to 'Letters written from my garden', 1853.

Lincoln's address on Zachary Taylor, delivered in the City Hall in Chicago on Thursday afternoon, July 25, 1850, contains the sentence: 'The Presidency, even to the most experienced politicians, is no bed of roses; and General Taylor, like others, found thorns within it. No human being can fill that station and escape censure.'

Illinois historian Neil Gale's Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal lists 'We can complain because rose bushes have thorns, or rejoice because thorn bushes have roses' among unfounded Lincoln quotations, stating there is no evidence Lincoln wrote or spoke it and citing the 1850 Zachary Taylor eulogy as his only roses-and-thorns remark.

Alphonse Karr (Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr) was a French critic, journalist and novelist, born 24 November 1808 and died 29 September 1890; he became editor of Le Figaro in 1839, founded the satirical monthly Les Guêpes, and after moving to Nice in 1855 practically founded the cut-flower trade on the French Riviera.
